title: Silbo Gomero – the whistle ‘language’ of the Canary Islands

Silbo Gomero – the whistle ‘language’ of the Canary Islands

La Gomera is one of the Canary Islands situated in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa. This small volcanic island is mountainous, with steep rocky slopes and deep, wooded ravines, rising to 1,487 metres at its highest peak. It is also home to the best known of the world’s whistle ‘languages’, a means of transmitting information over long distances which is perfectly adapted to the extreme terrain of the island.

This ‘language’, known as ‘Silbo’ or ‘Silbo Gomero’ – from the Spanish word for ‘whistle’ – is now shedding light on the language-processing abilities of the human brain, according to scientists. Researchers say that Silbo activates parts of the brain normally associated with spoken language, suggesting that the brain is remarkably flexible in its ability to interpret sounds as language.

‘Science has developed the idea of brain areas that are dedicated to language, and we are starting to understand the scope of signals that can be recognised as language,’ says David Corina, co-author of a recent study and associate professor of psychology at the University of Washington in Seattle.

Silbo is a substitute for Spanish, with individual words recoded into whistles which have high- and low-frequency tones. A whistler – or silbador – puts a finger in his or her mouth to increase the whistle’s pitch, while the other hand can be cupped to adjust the direction of the sound. ‘There is much more ambiguity in the whistled signal than in the spoken signal,’ explains lead researcher Manuel Carreiras, psychology professor at the University of La Laguna on the Canary island of Tenerife. Because whistled ‘words’ can be hard to distinguish, silbadores rely on repetition, as well as awareness of context, to make themselves understood.

The silbadores of Gomera are traditionally shepherds and other isolated mountain folk, and their novel means of staying in touch allows them to communicate over distances of up to 10 kilometres. Carreiras explains that silbadores are able to pass a surprising amount of information via their whistles. ‘In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled.’ Silbo has proved particularly useful when fires have occurred on the island and rapid communication across large areas has been vital.

The study team used neuroimaging equipment to contrast the brain activity of silbadores while listening to whistled and spoken Spanish. Results showed the left temporal lobe of the brain, which is usually associated with spoken language, was engaged during the processing of Silbo. The researchers found that other key regions in the brain’s frontal lobe also responded to the whistles, including those activated in response to sign language among deaf people. When the experiments were repeated with non-whistlers, however, activation was observed in all areas of the brain.

‘Our results provide more evidence about the flexibility of human capacity for language in a variety of forms,’ Corina says. ‘These data suggest that left-hemisphere language regions are uniquely adapted for communicative purposes, independent of the modality of signal. The non-Silbo speakers were not recognising Silbo as a language. They had nothing to grab onto, so multiple areas of their brains were activated.’

Carreiras says the origins of Silbo Gomero remain obscure, but that indigenous Canary Islanders, who were of North African origin, already had a whistled language when Spain conquered the volcanic islands in the 15th century. Whistled languages survive today in Papua New Guinea, Mexico, Vietnam, Guyana, China, Nepal, Senegal, and a few mountainous pockets in southern Europe. There are thought to be as many as 70 whistled languages still in use, though only 12 have been described and studied scientifically. This form of communication is an adaptation found among cultures where people are often isolated from each other, according to Julien Meyer, a researcher at the Institute of Human Sciences in Lyon, France. ‘They are mostly used in mountains or dense forests,’ he says. ‘Whistled languages are quite clearly defined and represent an original adaptation of the spoken language for the needs of isolated human groups.’

But with modern communication technology now widely available, researchers say whistled languages like Silbo are threatened with extinction. With dwindling numbers of Gomera islanders still fluent in the language, Canaries’ authorities are taking steps to try to ensure its survival. Since 1999, Silbo Gomero has been taught in all of the island’s elementary schools. In addition, locals are seeking assistance from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). ‘The local authorities are trying to get an award from the organisation to declare [Silbo Gomero] as something that should be preserved for humanity,’ Carreiras adds.

questions.prompt: La Gomera is the most mountainous of all the Canary Islands.
questions.evidence: This small volcanic island is mountainous, with steep rocky slopes and deep, wooded ravines, rising to 1,487 metres at its highest peak.
questions.distractors: No comparison with every other Canary Island is given. TRUE adds an unsupported superlative; FALSE would require proof that another island is more mountainous.

questions.prompt: Silbo is only appropriate for short and simple messages.
questions.evidence: ‘In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled.’
synonymSubstitutions: short and simple messages ↔ short commands
only appropriate ↔ any Spanish sentence could be whistled
questions.distractors: ‘Short commands’ tempts TRUE, but ‘any Spanish sentence’ directly contradicts ‘only’; the issue is explicit, so NOT GIVEN is excluded.

questions.prompt: In the brain-activity study, silbadores and non-whistlers produced different results.
questions.evidence: The researchers found that other key regions in the brain’s frontal lobe also responded to the whistles, including those activated in response to sign language among deaf people. When the experiments were repeated with non-whistlers, however, activation was observed in all areas of the brain.
synonymSubstitutions: different results ↔ key regions / all areas
questions.distractors: ‘However’ marks the explicit contrast. FALSE denies it, and NOT GIVEN ignores the reported results.

questions.prompt: The Spanish introduced Silbo to the islands in the 15th century.
questions.evidence: indigenous Canary Islanders, who were of North African origin, already had a whistled language when Spain conquered the volcanic islands in the 15th century
questions.distractors: The date and Spain tempt TRUE, but ‘already had’ shows the language predated conquest; the chronology excludes NOT GIVEN.

questions.prompt: There is precise data available regarding all of the whistle languages in existence today.
questions.evidence: There are thought to be as many as 70 whistled languages still in use, though only 12 have been described and studied scientifically.
synonymSubstitutions: in existence today ↔ still in use
precise data regarding all ↔ only 12 studied scientifically
questions.distractors: ‘As many as 70’ is an estimate and only 12 are studied, contradicting precise data for all; this is stated, so NOT GIVEN is excluded.

questions.prompt: The children of Gomera now learn Silbo.
questions.evidence: Since 1999, Silbo Gomero has been taught in all of the island’s elementary schools.
synonymSubstitutions: children of Gomera ↔ island’s elementary schools
now learn ↔ has been taught since 1999
questions.distractors: The school programme directly supports the statement; FALSE contradicts it and NOT GIVEN overlooks it.

questions.prompt: high- and low-frequency tones represent different sounds in Spanish 20 __________
questions.evidence: Silbo is a substitute for Spanish, with individual words recoded into whistles which have high- and low-frequency tones.
synonymSubstitutions: represent different sounds ↔ recoded into whistles
questions.distractors: Whistles are the recoded form and tones are frequencies; the plural item represented is words.

questions.prompt: pitch of whistle is controlled using silbador’s 21 __________
questions.evidence: A whistler – or silbador – puts a finger in his or her mouth to increase the whistle’s pitch
questions.distractors: Mouth is the location, but finger is the instrument; hand controls direction in the next note.

questions.prompt: 22 __________ is changed with a cupped hand
questions.evidence: the other hand can be cupped to adjust the direction of the sound
synonymSubstitutions: with a cupped hand ↔ hand can be cupped
questions.distractors: Pitch is changed with a finger; sound is general, while direction is the precise property adjusted.

questions.prompt: in everyday use for the transmission of brief 23 __________
questions.evidence: ‘In daily life they use whistles to communicate short commands, but any Spanish sentence could be whistled.’
questions.distractors: Sentence describes wider capability; routine use is specifically for commands. Information is too broad.

questions.prompt: can relay essential information quickly, e.g. to inform people about 24 __________
questions.evidence: Silbo has proved particularly useful when fires have occurred on the island and rapid communication across large areas has been vital.
questions.distractors: Areas is the reach and island the location; fires are the emergency communicated about.

questions.prompt: future under threat because of new 25 __________
questions.evidence: But with modern communication technology now widely available, researchers say whistled languages like Silbo are threatened with extinction.
synonymSubstitutions: future under threat ↔ threatened with extinction
questions.distractors: Communication modifies technology; extinction is the outcome, not the cause.

questions.prompt: Canaries’ authorities hoping to receive a UNESCO 26 __________ to help preserve it
questions.evidence: ‘The local authorities are trying to get an award from the organisation to declare [Silbo Gomero] as something that should be preserved for humanity,’ Carreiras adds.
synonymSubstitutions: hoping to receive ↔ trying to get
questions.distractors: Assistance is a general request, but the quotation and article ‘a’ identify award; organisation refers to UNESCO itself.
